name: Grace Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal workday involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am forty-three, a lead carpenter with a trade certificate, and I set out stairs and roof joins on building sites. I use an AI drawing assistant most mornings to compare quantities, then put the phone away and mark the timber myself. The crew asks me to fix the difficult corners, though my pay is low for a lead. My partner and I have two schoolchildren, a mortgage and less than a month of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the drawing assistant is handy for routine counts but the stairs still need a careful hand. A building stair is not safe because an AI drawing says its risers match.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be relieved that my site skill still earns wages, but our money is fragile. Even a small delay in a paid job leaves the mortgage close to the edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would carry on leading the stair crew and use the AI assistant for counts as I do now. I would check its figures against the actual opening and save a little new money from each full paid week after bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the cash we have, even in this quiet picture. The tool itself is already part of my day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you check before cutting a stair stringer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The actual floor height and the opening, twice. A neat digital drawing cannot tell me whether yesterday’s concrete is level.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would new savings come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only from a full paid week after the mortgage, food and school transport. We have less than a month saved now, so I would record each real transfer.

say: I would **keep** using AI for stair quantities and verify every building opening myself.
I would **tell** the crew that the drawing is a starting point, never a safety check.
think: My **carpenter** skill still brings work, but the mortgage leaves little margin for a missed week.
**Existing** daily AI use does not mean I trust a drawing more than a measured riser.
do: **Keep** leading stair fitting and compare AI counts with measured openings.
**Save** new money from full paid weeks after mortgage and school bills.
feel: **Uneasy** about thin savings despite stable hands-on work.
S0.quote: A building stair is not safe because an AI drawing says its risers match.
fieldNote: **Grace** uses AI every day for counts, then checks each physical stair opening before cutting.
Her **strong** craft standing coexists with low wages and savings below one month of expenses.

steps.text: Keep leading stair fitting and checking AI counts
Save new pay from full site weeks after bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that smarter planning could cut office delays, but we need to see what it does to our paid site days. The drawing assistant already helps me count; I would learn its new scheduling controls. A faster AI schedule might shorten the carpenter’s paid week before it shortens a building job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am worried the builder will promise the same number of stair jobs with fewer paid crew hours. My partner’s income helps, but a shortened week from either of us would hit the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the crew schedule and rate in writing, then practice the new AI scheduling feature on a job we have already measured. I would keep my stair shifts and save any new pay from extra work, if it actually arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious about hours, not frightened of learning software. I know the builder can choose to share a saving or keep it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show the crew before using the new feature?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare its proposed delivery day and timber count with one completed stair job. If it misses a site delay, I would flag it to the planner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the builder offers fewer days?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for other paid stair work first. I would check a posted local lead vacancy only if its wage covers our mortgage, though there are few nearby.

say: I would **learn** the new scheduling controls and test them on a measured stair job.
I would **ask** how faster planning affects crew hours and the wage rate.
think: A **shortened** paid week would reach our mortgage quickly despite my strong site skill.
**Software** efficiency does not decide how the builder shares the savings.
do: **Practice** new AI scheduling controls on a completed stair job.
**Request** written site schedule and wage terms while keeping paid shifts.
**Save** pay from additional stair shifts after household bills.
feel: **Anxious** about realistic paid-hour cuts, with a way to check terms.
S1.quote: A faster AI schedule might shorten the carpenter’s paid week before it shortens a building job.
fieldNote: She is **quick** to learn new AI controls, but tests them against a physical site record.
Her **own** paid hours could shrink soon, making anxiety consistent with the thin household buffer.

steps.text: Practice new AI scheduling controls on measured stair work
Keep paid stair shifts while checking written terms
Save new pay from extra stair shifts after bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say full thinking AI in 2028 can draw and price stairs when I am forty-five, but our hands still fit them then. I will be forty-eight when the hands-on robots arrive around 2031. A robot can fit a straight building stair in 2031 while my mortgage still wants a full carpenter’s wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the builder to need fewer paid carpenters once robots fit standard stairs. My difficult joins may keep some work, yet there are few other nearby jobs and less than one month of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use AI now to document the odd staircase failures I solve, then ask the builder for a paid trial checking robot-fitted stairs. If hours fall after robots arrive, I would cut optional spending and seek a posted local checking role only if the wage covers mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am alarmed because I think a large part of our paid week could disappear. I have been awake calculating whether the mortgage could survive that loss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your work record show that an AI drawing does not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Photographs of the crooked opening, my measured correction and the final tread height. I could show a checker exactly why the drawing changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take an unpaid robot trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A trial must replace a paid shift or pay its own hours, because an unpaid week would consume what little cushion we have.

say: **Thinking** AI changes stair drawings in 2028; hands-on robots threaten standard fitting around 2031.
I would **seek** a paid checking trial using records of my difficult stair joins.
think: I **expect** major paid-hour loss on standard stairs and lie awake over the mortgage.
A **real** local vacancy with adequate wages matters more than being called a robot expert.
do: **Document** awkward stair corrections with AI and measured photographs now.
**Ask** builder for paid robot-stair checking trial before 2031.
**Apply** for posted nearby checker role only if pay covers mortgage and school costs.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major paid-hour loss and sleepless mortgage calculations.
S2.quote: A robot can fit a straight building stair in 2031 while my mortgage still wants a full carpenter’s wage.
fieldNote: Her **daily** AI skill helps document craft judgment but cannot replace lost paid fitting hours.
She **expects** major income loss after the 2031 robot arrival and says the mortgage calculation keeps her awake.

steps.text: Document awkward stair corrections with existing AI and measured photographs
Keep paid carpentry during trial if builder pays trial hours
Apply for posted local checking job with bill-covering wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew we have until 2031 for thinking AI and about 2034 for hands-on robots. At forty-eight and fifty-one, I could train for structural checks while still earning on the stair crew. A structural inspection certificate cannot pay my mortgage unless a local builder posts a paid job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not pay for that training myself while our savings are so thin. I also need a posted local checking job, because a certificate with no paid place to use it would not carry the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the builder to fund a practical structural inspection course on paid time and enroll only if both are agreed. In the first year after 2031, I would keep the stair shifts and apply after completing training only for posted nearby inspection jobs with a household-covering wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about standard stair work shrinking, but five years lets me prepare more deliberately. I can make a decision when there are real terms on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why inspection instead of more advanced AI drawing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already use AI for drawings. I want the formal right to inspect tread heights and handrails on site, where the physical mistakes are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course is funded but the hours are unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for paid release or keep working. Our mortgage cannot wait through unpaid training, however useful the certificate looks.

say: The 2031 **thinking** change comes before site robots around 2034.
I would **take** formal physical inspection training only if the course and time are paid.
think: A **course** has value only alongside a posted local inspection role with adequate pay.
My **current** AI practice does not give me a formal inspection credential.
do: **Enroll** in structural inspection course only with full funding and paid release.
**Keep** paid stair shifts through training and the 2031 thinking change.
**Apply** after completion to posted nearby inspector job with household-covering wage.
feel: **Anxious** about later stair-hour loss, with time for a conditional route.
S3.quote: A structural inspection certificate cannot pay my mortgage unless a local builder posts a paid job.
fieldNote: She **distinguishes** current AI use from new formal site inspection training.
**Paid** release, course funding, a real vacancy and adequate wages all control her route.

steps.text: Enroll in funded inspection course with paid release
Keep paid stair shifts through training
Apply for posted local inspector role with adequate wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my children that thinking AI arrives when I am fifty-three in 2036, and capable site robots around 2039 when I am fifty-six. That is time to teach safer stair work, if someone pays for the teaching. Ten years of warning about building robots will not fill the mortgage account after an unpaid week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could see myself leading apprentices through actual measurements, but I will not assume teaching jobs appear. The low wage and our thin savings are pressures now, ten years before any robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading stair work and put a new amount from each full paid week into an emergency account after bills. If the builder funds assessor training on paid time, I would complete it and seek a posted nearby teaching or assessor role only at a wage that covers the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about current money and uneasy about the distant machines. More warning helps only if the working years between are paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would make an apprentice measure the first and last riser in a real building before trusting a generated drawing. A small error repeats up a whole flight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move the family for a teaching offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on a rumour. With two children in school and a mortgage, I would first require a written local vacancy and a wage that pays our bills.

say: A **decade** gives me time to save new wages and teach measured stair work.
I would **require** a paid teaching or assessor role rather than assume one exists.
think: **Thin** savings and lower pay remain household risks long before 2039.
**Training** needs funding and paid time; a later move needs a posted vacancy and adequate wage.
do: **Save** new amounts from full paid stair weeks after household bills.
**Complete** funded assessor training only if the builder pays training time.
**Apply** for posted nearby assessor role only with a household-covering wage.
feel: **Anxious** about present cash pressure and uneasy about later robots.
S4.quote: Ten years of warning about building robots will not fill the mortgage account after an unpaid week.
fieldNote: Her **adaptive** outlook produces early savings and conditional training, not an assumed teaching job.
**New** savings come from paid wages; course fees, paid hours and actual local job terms remain constraints.

steps.text: Save new pay from full stair weeks after bills
Complete funded assessor course with paid training hours
Apply for posted local assessor job with adequate pay

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast picture worries me most. I expect a large loss of standard stair hours after robots arrive around 2031, and I have lain awake over the mortgage. A paid checking trial and a real nearby job at enough wages would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the hours in every attractive training plan are paid. I can learn fast, but a family with less than a month saved cannot pay its mortgage in enthusiasm. I can teach an AI to count stair treads, but it cannot make an unpaid training week affordable.

headlineQuote: I can teach an AI to count stair treads, but it cannot make an unpaid training week affordable.
portrait: **Grace** is a forty-three-year-old lead carpenter with a trade certificate, two schoolchildren and a mortgage.
She is **among** the best at stair fitting and uses AI every day for drawings and quantities.
Her **low** pay, less than one month saved and few nearby jobs make paid hours critical.
She **learns** new controls early but requires paid trials, funded training and posted adequate local roles before moving.
biggestWorry: The **fast** 2028/2031 picture brings expected major loss of paid standard stair work and sleepless mortgage calculations.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid** robot-checking trials, funded training on paid time and a posted nearby job paying household bills would help.
